html:
The Erlitou culture was an early Bronze Age society of the middle Yellow River valley in China, named after its main site near Yanshi in Henan, close to Luoyang. Older estimates date it about 1900 to 1500 BCE; radiocarbon studies since 2007 suggest a narrower 1750 to 1500 BCE.

Most archaeologists consider Erlitou the first state in China. The site had:

  • a palace area with large rammed-earth halls and courtyards, surrounded by a wall
  • a grid of roads, the oldest known in China
  • workshops for bronze, turquoise and bone
  • the first Chinese bronze ritual vessels, cast in pottery moulds, a technique that later Chinese bronze work built on

The big question is whether Erlitou was the Xia dynasty, the first dynasty in Chinese tradition, founded by Yu the Great who tamed the floods. Erlitou is in the right place and the right time. Chinese archaeologists generally treat it as late Xia. Many Western scholars say that is premature: no writing has been found there, so there is no way to know what its rulers called themselves.

Erlitou grew out of the Longshan cultures after their collapse. Around 1600 BCE its centre declined, and a new walled city rose nearby at Yanshi and then at Zhengzhou. These belong to the Erligang culture, usually identified with the early Shang, the first dynasty known from its own writing.
